## Gas-informed parent-fluid reconstruction, database sensitivity, and flowpath trace


::: {.callout-note}
## What this section covers, in sequence

This subsection covers one connected analysis built across several
steps, in this order: (1) a steam-loss and gas-add-back correction
reconstructs the fissure's deep "parent fluid" using the one available
real fissure gas sample; (2) the identical method is also applied,
diagnostically, to the resort tank, but the well feeding the resort
tank is pumped with a true, intermittent air-lift pump, a mechanically
forced aeration process the method's own steam-loss physics does not
represent, so the resulting "agreement" between the two reconstructions
is reported but not relied on as evidence; (3) a six-database
sensitivity sweep is run on the resort-tank reconstruction because its
gas-equilibration step failed to converge on this project's default
database; (4) that divergence is root-caused to the resort tank's own
high measured starting pH (9.0 versus the fissure's 8.3) -- itself very
plausibly a direct consequence of the air-lift pump's forced aeration,
not database choice, gas-load size, or a property of the deep reservoir
fluid; (5) the fissure's reconstructed parent fluid (not the resort
tank's) is then used as an end-member in real PHREEQC inverse modeling
against both targets, which finds zero feasible solutions -- attributed
to a known PHREEQC numerical quirk, not a geochemical rejection of the
end-member; and (6) the reconstructed fissure parent fluid and the
as-measured chemistry at every other node, including the resort tank's
own as-pumped composition, are traced along a full flowpath from parent
fluid to the downstream creek. Each step is reported with its own real
result below.
:::

**A gas-informed parent-fluid reconstruction.** Applying the method
above to sample 816 (the fissure) gives a steam-loss fraction of 19.4
percent (reservoir 173.4 degrees Celsius, measured discharge 67.0
degrees Celsius), a reconstructed parent chloride of 657 mg/L (below
the measured 815 mg/L, as boiling concentrates the residual liquid),
and -- once the reconstructed fluid is re-equilibrated with NV26-1's
real gas composition at reservoir pressure (8.7 atmospheres) -- a
substantially more acidic parent pH (5.5, versus 8.3 measured) and
calcite/dolomite saturation indices that flip from mildly supersaturated
to clearly undersaturated. This is the expected direction for a deep,
gas-charged fluid that has not yet degassed: carbonate scaling is a
surface/shallow phenomenon as carbon dioxide escapes and pH rises, not
a deep-reservoir one, shown in @fig-parentfluid. Applying the identical
method to the resort-tank sample (815) gives a similar steam-loss
fraction (20.8 percent) and a parent chloride within 2.3 percent of the
fissure's own reconstructed parent (657 vs. 672 mg/L) -- closer than the
two samples' raw measured values (815 vs. 849 mg/L). This agreement is
reported, not relied upon: the resort-tank well is pumped with a true,
intermittent air-lift pump, a forced-aeration process this method's
steam-loss physics does not represent, so its reconstructed "parent"
is not a trustworthy estimate of a deep fluid, and the tight Cl
agreement could just as easily be a coincidence of applying an
inapplicable correction as it could be real evidence of a shared
source. Potassium, sulfate, lithium, and strontium converge less
tightly (9-15 percent apart even after correction), which could reflect
either minor water-rock reaction differences along slightly different
flow paths, real sampling/analytical variability, or the resort tank's
pumping artifact -- not resolved further here. The resort-tank sample's
own gas-equilibration step did not converge (a real PHREEQC limitation
at this fluid's measured pH of 9.0 combined with the imposed acid-gas
load, logged to
`parent_fluid_diagnostics.csv` rather than hidden), so its reconstructed
parent pH and saturation indices are not reported -- only its
conservative-species concentrations, which do not depend on that step.

::: {.callout-note}
A field-temperature unit bug (the project's Fluke field thermometer
reports Fahrenheit, mislabeled as Celsius downstream of ingestion) was
found and fixed after these reconstructions were first run, and every
number above reflects the corrected temperatures. The steam-loss
fractions and reconstructed parent chloride changed materially (the
fissure's steam-loss fraction moved from an originally-miscalculated
4.2 percent to the corrected 19.4 percent, for example), but the
qualitative conclusion -- the two independently reconstructed parent
fluids converge more tightly than the raw measured values do -- holds
under both the original and corrected temperatures.
:::

```{r fig-parentfluid}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/parent_fluid_comparison.png",
  "A. Measured versus gas-informed reconstructed parent-fluid composition for the fissure sample. B. The resulting conservative-chloride thermal mixing fraction for three real Lower Sinter Terrace samples, computed with the measured fluid versus the reconstructed parent fluid as the thermal end-member.",
  alt = "Two-panel figure: bar chart comparing measured and parent-fluid concentrations of ten conservative species; point plot comparing mixing fractions under two end-member choices for three target samples.",
  id = "fig-parentfluid"
)
```


**Does the choice of thermodynamic database matter here, especially
given the resort-tank fluid's convergence failure?** Database choice
turned out to be a symptom, not the real cause. Re-running the
resort-tank parent fluid's gas-equilibration step against all six
PHREEQC databases registered in this project, with the corrected field
temperature, finds that the resort tank now fails to converge on
**every one** of the six databases at its own real, measured field pH
(9.0), shown in @fig-dbsensitivity -- a larger, more consistent failure
than first found (before the temperature correction, two of the six
databases had converged, landing on a dramatically more acidic parent
pH of approximately 2.0-2.1; the corrected, larger steam-loss fraction
increases the imposed gas load enough that even those two now fail
outright). Tracking this down directly (controlled PHREEQC experiments,
not guessed) rules out two plausible-looking explanations before
finding the real one: swapping boron in or out of the fissure's own
solution changes its final pH by less than 0.01 units (boron is
excluded from the resort-tank solution only because including it
prevents the *initial* solution from converging at all, a separate,
already-documented issue -- not the driver of the acidification
difference); and the two fluids' conservative-species concentrations
are too similar to explain a gap this large. The real cause is the
two samples' different **measured field pH**: 9.0 for the resort tank
versus 8.3 for the fissure. Re-running the resort tank's exact real
chemistry with only its starting pH changed to 8.3 converges cleanly
on all three general-purpose databases tested (`phreeqc.dat`, LLNL, and
`wateq4f.dat`) and lands within 0.1 pH units of the fissure's own
result (5.44-5.55 versus the fissure's 5.48-5.60 across the same three
databases) -- confirming that a 0.7-unit difference in starting pH, not
the choice of thermodynamic database, drives both the convergence
failure and the acidic divergence, now demonstrated even more starkly
than before the temperature correction (the resort tank fails on every
database at its own real pH, not just three of six). Mechanistically, a
solution starting at pH 9 has already converted most of its alkalinity
to carbonate rather than bicarbonate, leaving much less carbonate
buffering capacity before the same imposed gas load drives the system
into a strongly acidic, weakly buffered regime. This is reported as a
resolved, mechanistically understood sensitivity, not an open question:
the conservative-species correction (chloride, sodium, and so on) was
never in doubt and is unaffected by any of this; the resort tank's own
re-equilibrated pH and saturation indices, as reported above, should be
read as sensitive to its unusually high measured field pH specifically,
not to a database artifact. That high starting pH itself has a specific,
mechanistically plausible real-world cause rather than being an
unexplained property of the fluid: the well feeding the resort tank is
pumped with a true, intermittent air-lift pump, which forces atmospheric
air through the water column to lift it. Stripping carbon dioxide via
forced air contact raises pH in essentially the same direction as
natural degassing does, so the resort tank's elevated pH plausibly
reflects pumping, not an unusually large amount of natural boiling or
an unusually alkaline deep source -- a more parsimonious explanation
than treating the convergence failure purely as a numerical sensitivity
to be worked around.

As a direct check on one remaining candidate explanation, the amount
of gas imposed on each parent fluid is scaled to each sample's own
alkalinity rather than applied as a fixed total regardless of buffering
capacity. Because the resort tank's and fissure's alkalinities differ
by only about 6 percent, this changes the imposed gas load by a similar
small amount and leaves the result essentially unchanged: the resort
tank still fails to converge on every database tested, now including
the two (`phreeqc.dat`, `wateq4f.dat`) that had converged before the
temperature correction was applied. This is a real, if negative,
confirmation rather than a wasted step -- it rules out gas-load sizing
as a contributing factor and leaves the resort tank's unusually high
measured field pH -- itself most plausibly a product of its air-lift
pump, not a deep-fluid property -- as the sole identified driver.

```{r fig-dbsensitivity}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/parent_fluid_database_sensitivity.png",
  "A. Gas-equilibration convergence for both real water-gas pairings, across all six PHREEQC databases registered in this project. B. Reconstructed parent-fluid pH for every database that converged. The resort tank's divergence traces to its higher measured field pH (9.0 vs. 8.3), not database choice -- plausibly itself a consequence of the resort well's true air-lift pump -- see text.",
  alt = "Two-panel figure: tile plot showing convergence status by database and sample; point plot showing reconstructed pH by database for the two samples.",
  id = "fig-dbsensitivity"
)
```

**Feeding the reconstructed parent fluid into real inverse modeling.**
Running this project's existing PHREEQC inverse-modeling framework
(end-members: the fissure's reconstructed parent fluid -- not the
resort tank's, for the reasons given above -- and the meteoric
reference well; candidate phases: calcite, quartz, chalcedony) against
the two real target samples with complete chemistry (SBW_0001,
SBW_0002, both used as-measured) finds zero feasible
mixing-plus-mineral-transfer solutions for either target. This is not read as a geochemical rejection of the
parent-fluid end-member -- the raw PHREEQC output traces the failure to
the same tiny (on the order of 1e-9), numerically spurious residual on
an unused trace redox couple (chlorine or carbon oxidation states that
play no real role in this chemistry) already documented as a known
PHREEQC execution-plumbing limitation in this project's own synthetic
self-tests. Reported plainly as a real, current limitation of the
inverse-modeling tool for this specific end-member pairing, not
silently retried until something "worked." A separate, independent
inverse-modeling attempt against SBW_0001 directly (end-members: the
fissure and SBRR rather than the reconstructed parent fluid; candidate
phases: calcite, dolomite), re-run after the field-temperature
correction, now finds a genuine feasible solution once the analytical
uncertainty is loosened to 12 percent or more -- a materially different
and more informative result than the pre-fix search, which found none
at any uncertainty up to 15 percent. At the standard 5 percent
uncertainty the model is infeasible for several elements at once
(alkalinity, carbon, calcium, and potassium); at 10 and 11 percent a
single, cleanly shrinking calcium residual remains (2.5e-4 mol at 10
percent, 1.1e-4 mol at 11 percent); at 12 percent this residual clears
and PHREEQC reports one real feasible model: a 70.6/29.4 percent
fissure/SBRR mixture plus a net *dissolution* of 4.0e-4 mol calcite and
1.3e-4 mol dolomite. At 15 percent uncertainty a second feasible
solution is found with a somewhat different mixture (65.8/34.2 percent)
and similar net dissolution. This is a real, quantitative point of
agreement with the forward titration result below: both methods
independently converge on net calcite-plus-dolomite *dissolution* on
the order of a few times 1e-4 mol along this flowpath, not
precipitation. Read together, a feasible two-end-member-plus-carbonate
model for SBW_0001 exists, but only once the uncertainty allowed on the
underlying chemical analyses is relaxed beyond this project's usual 5
percent default -- consistent with real analytical uncertainty on these
samples' major-ion measurements being larger than typically assumed, a
genuine and testable hypothesis for a tighter future sampling round
rather than a modeling dead end.

**A forward alternative: titrating calcite and dolomite instead of
asking the solver to search for them.** Because the inverse search
above is only feasible at a loosened uncertainty tolerance, a
complementary, better-posed question is to run the reaction forward at
the standard, un-loosened analytical uncertainty: mix the fissure and
SBRR at their real, already-computed conservative mixing fraction, then
explicitly step calcite and dolomite mass transfer -- both net
precipitation and net dissolution -- and see what the resulting
chemistry trajectory looks like, shown in @fig-reactionpath. The result
is a genuine interior optimum, not an edge artifact of the explored
range: a modest net *dissolution* of calcite and dolomite (on the order
of one-tenth of a millimole, 1.17e-4 mol combined) brings the combined
calcium, magnesium, and alkalinity error down from roughly 45 to 48
percent at pure conservative mixing to about 23 percent at the best
fit. That is a real, substantial improvement over mixing alone, but it
does not fully reconcile the target -- alkalinity in particular never
reaches its observed value anywhere in the titrated range. Chloride
stays exactly conservative across every step, confirming the titration
moves only the carbonate system, as intended. Read together, the
inverse and forward results now reinforce each other on both the sign
and the rough magnitude of the needed correction: net calcite-plus-
dolomite dissolution, not precipitation, order 1e-4 mol. The inverse
search needs a looser uncertainty tolerance to call this feasible in a
strict least-squares sense; the forward titration shows the same
direction and size of correction brings the fit most of the way there
even without loosening anything, with alkalinity as the one component
that resists full reconciliation either way -- a genuine part of the
answer, not a dead end, and a concrete target for tighter future
alkalinity measurements at this specific well.

```{r fig-reactionpath}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/reaction_path_titration.png",
  "Forward PHREEQC REACTION-path titration of calcite and dolomite into the fissure+SBRR conservative mix, compared against SBW_0001's real observed Ca/Mg/Alkalinity (dashed lines) and the best-fit reaction progress (dotted line).",
  alt = "Five-panel figure: calcium, magnesium, alkalinity, calcite saturation index, and dolomite saturation index, each plotted against net reaction progress, with a dashed horizontal reference line for the real observed value and a dotted vertical line marking the best-fit reaction progress.",
  id = "fig-reactionpath"
)
```

**Running the same titration against the three real Low Sinter Terrace
springs tells a more complicated story than the saturation-index-only
view suggested.** The earlier forward-mixing figure, based only on
calcite and dolomite saturation index and pH, showed the three springs
(SBS_0001, SBS_0002, SBS_0003) sitting much closer to the pure-mixing
curve than SBW_0001. Running the identical forward titration against
each spring directly, using the full Ca/Mg/Alkalinity mass balance
rather than saturation index alone, does not fully confirm that
picture, shown in @fig-reactionpath-comparison. SBS_0002 needs almost
no reaction correction at all, consistent with the earlier read.
SBS_0003 needs a small correction and reaches a good fit (19.7 percent
combined error, the best of the four real targets). SBS_0001, however,
shows the **worst** fit of all four targets even after titration (44.5
percent), despite needing a comparatively modest reaction-progress
correction -- its real calcium sits well above anything the explored
titration range can reach, while its real alkalinity sits below the
titration curve's own value at every explored point, including the
most negative (net-precipitation) step the real Ca/Mg/alkalinity pool
can physically support. These two demands pull in opposite directions
and cannot both be satisfied by this simple two-phase model over a
physically available range, not because the search was cut short.
Chloride stays exactly conservative at every step for every target, so
this is not an artifact of the conservative-tracer assumption itself.
SBW_0001 remains the target needing by far the largest correction and
showing the largest absolute improvement, but it is no longer the only
target this simple model struggles to explain -- SBS_0001 does too, for
a different, specific reason.

```{r fig-reactionpath-comparison}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/reaction_path_fit_comparison.png",
  "Combined Ca/Mg/Alkalinity fit error at pure conservative mixing versus each target's own best-fit reaction progress, across all five real downgradient targets.",
  alt = "Dumbbell plot comparing fit error (percent) at pure mixing versus best-fit reaction progress for five samples: SBW_0001, SBW_0002, SBS_0001, SBS_0002, and SBS_0003.",
  id = "fig-reactionpath-comparison"
)
```

**A fifth real target: the resort tank (SBW_0002), run with a necessary
adjustment.** SBW_0002's own stored conservative mixing fraction against
the fissure and SBRR is 1.043, slightly above the valid 0 to 1 range --
a real, already-documented finding (this project's own earlier work)
that SBW_0002 is *more* concentrated than the fissure reference itself,
not a new problem. A fraction outside this range cannot be represented
as a real mixture of the two named end-members, so the fraction is
clamped to 1.0 (pure fissure end-member, no meteoric dilution) before
running the titration, with the modeling implication stated explicitly
rather than silently worked around: the question being asked shifts from
"does mixing plus reaction explain this sample" to "does reaction alone,
starting from the pure thermal end-member, explain the small remaining
gap." Under that explicitly adjusted question, SBW_0002 fits extremely
well: a combined Ca/Mg/Alkalinity error of only 4.6 percent at a tiny
net precipitation (on the order of one-millionth of a mole), by far the
best fit of any real target tested on this flowpath, shown in
@fig-reactionpath-comparison. This titration uses SBW_0002's real
as-measured (as-pumped) composition throughout, not a reconstructed
parent fluid, so the air-lift pump's effect on gas chemistry and pH
does not bear on it: calcium, magnesium, and alkalinity are not the
species an air-lift pump would be expected to alter, so this excellent
fit is read as a genuine, trustworthy result about how closely
SBW_0002's major-ion chemistry resembles the fissure's, independent of
the separate pH/gas-equilibration concerns raised above.

**Does a sulfate phase, or a different meteoric input, resolve
SBS_0001's own tension?** SBS_0001's real chemistry gave a specific,
testable lead: it has the highest sulfate (187 milligrams per liter) and
lowest alkalinity of the four original downgradient targets, the classic
gypsum or anhydrite signature a carbonate-only titration cannot
reproduce, since calcite and dolomite tie calcium directly to carbonate,
not sulfate. Two real hypotheses were tested directly, shown in
@fig-sbs0001-sensitivity: adding anhydrite, gypsum, or anhydrite plus
fluorite as additional candidate phases (fluorite tested because
SBS_0001 also has real, if more modest, fluoride data), and separately,
mixing with a different, higher-sulfate shallow water instead of SBRR,
using two real candidates with usable chemistry already in this
database (Tick Spring and Jumbo Grade Spring, both from Mariner and
Janik 1995, neither with a coordinate on file -- the same documented
limitation already noted for Jumbo Grade Spring). Scored on the same
fixed calcium, magnesium, and alkalinity basis as the baseline, for a
fair comparison, every variant improves on the baseline's 44.5 percent
error somewhat: anhydrite and gypsum each reach 40.3 percent, anhydrite
plus fluorite reaches 36.6 percent, Jumbo Grade Spring reaches 39.0
percent, and Tick Spring reaches 33.4 percent, the best single result on
this fixed metric. None fully resolves the tension, and the best result
achieved is still notably worse than SBS_0002's own 39.4 percent or
SBS_0003's own 19.7 percent baseline fits. A further, genuinely
informative wrinkle: when fluorite's own real fluoride prediction is
honestly included in the score (it was not, in the first pass -- a real
bug, since fixed, where fluoride was never added to PHREEQC's own
requested output list), the anhydrite-plus-fluorite variant gets
noticeably *worse* (50.8 percent), showing fluorite does not actually
explain real fluoride well on its own, while the combined variant
(anhydrite, fluorite, and the Tick Spring end-member together) becomes
the single best-fitting result of any tested, at 30.6 percent. The two
hypotheses do not simply stack in an obvious way, and the ranking
depends on which real chemistry is actually checked -- reported here in
full rather than rounded off to the most convenient-looking number.

```{r fig-sbs0001-sensitivity}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/sbs0001_sensitivity_comparison.png",
  "SBS_0001 sensitivity test: best-fit combined Ca/Mg/Alkalinity error across the baseline titration, three additional-phase variants, two alternate-meteoric-end-member variants, and one combined variant.",
  alt = "Horizontal bar chart ranking seven real model variants for sample SBS_0001 by best-fit RMSE percent, from the baseline at 44.5 percent down to the Tick Spring alternate end-member at 33.4 percent.",
  id = "fig-sbs0001-sensitivity"
)
```

**Close on a map, far apart chemically.** SBS_0001 and SBW_0001 sit only
109 meters apart by their own real coordinates, shown in
@fig-proximity-map, yet behave about as differently as any two real
targets on this flowpath can: SBS_0001 is the worst-fitting target
tested (even after every sensitivity variant above), while SBW_0001
needs the largest reaction-progress correction of the original four
targets but also shows one of the largest real improvements once that
correction is applied. This is a concrete, mappable instance of the
principle already stated in this proposal's discussion of modeling
assumptions: physical proximity does not imply shared chemistry or a
shared flow path, and a defensible model has to be built from which
samples are genuinely chemically alike, not which ones happen to sit
close together.

```{r fig-proximity-map}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/lst_proximity_map.png",
  "Real lat/lon positions of the seven flowpath samples, with the five real downgradient targets colored and sized by their own best-fit reaction-path RMSE.",
  alt = "Map of seven points with latitude and longitude axes, two grey triangles for the fissure and SBRR reference end-members, and five colored circles for the real downgradient targets sized by fit error.",
  id = "fig-proximity-map"
)
```

**A real Piper diagram, independent of any PHREEQC modeling.** As a
direct, model-free check of the sulfate hypothesis above, a trilinear
Piper diagram was built from the same seven samples' real mg/L
chemistry converted to charge-equivalent percentages, shown in
@fig-piper. The honest result is a real, if slightly deflating,
negative one: SBS_0001 does not visibly separate from SBS_0002 or
SBS_0003 toward the anion triangle's sulfate corner. Chloride dominates
the anion budget so heavily in every real thermal sample on this
flowpath that SBS_0001's real, absolute sulfate excess (187 versus
63 to 167 milligrams per liter at the other targets) does not translate
into a large shift in charge-equivalent percentage terms. The diagram
still does real, useful work: it visually separates SBRR from the
thermal cluster exactly as expected, and groups the thermal samples
together on both the cation and anion triangles, a plain visual
confirmation of the facies picture already established statistically in
Chapter 4's hierarchical clustering and principal-components work.

```{r fig-piper}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/lst_piper_diagram.png",
  "Trilinear Piper diagram, built directly from real mg/L chemistry, for the fissure, SBRR, SBW_0001, SBW_0002, and the three real Low Sinter Terrace springs.",
  alt = "Standard Piper diagram with a cation triangle, an anion triangle, and a central diamond, with seven colored points for the seven real flowpath samples.",
  id = "fig-piper"
)
```

**Tracing the flowpath from parent fluid to the downstream creek.**
Putting the two reconstructed parent fluids, the as-measured fissure
and resort-tank chemistry, a nearby Lower Sinter Terrace well
(SBW_0001), and the two real Steamboat Creek chloride-mass-balance
stations (SBRR, then downstream SBBV) on one real flowpath, shown in
@fig-evolution, gives a coherent, data-supported picture: chloride,
sodium, silica, and boron all decline in the same order along the
flowpath (parent/fissure/resort-tank high, SBW_0001 roughly half,
SBRR near background, SBBV measurably higher than SBRR again) -- the
same real chloride-flux difference between SBRR and SBBV that already
drives this project's own thermal-discharge estimate
(`chloride_mass_balance.R`), now shown constituent by constituent.
pH rises from the reconstructed parent (acidic) through the measured,
partly degassed discharge points (alkaline) to the creek (near-neutral
to mildly alkaline), consistent with progressive carbon dioxide loss.
Calcite saturation is undersaturated at the reconstructed parent,
mildly supersaturated at the two measured discharge points, and most
supersaturated at the nearby well and downstream creek -- a real,
specific illustration of where calcite scaling risk is highest along
this flow path. The quartz geothermometer declines smoothly and
plausibly along the same sequence (118 and 99 degrees Celsius at the
two warmest points, down to 53-62 degrees Celsius at the creek
stations); the sodium/potassium geothermometer does **not** behave
this way at the two creek stations (physically implausible values of
195-255 degrees Celsius), a known, already-documented artifact of
applying that geothermometer to dilute, non-thermal water -- shown for
transparency, not as a real reservoir-temperature estimate at those two
points. Delta-18-O and delta-2-H tell a complementary story: both
creek stations sit close to each other and more isotopically depleted
than the fissure or resort-tank water, consistent with the real
thermal inflow being a small enough fraction of total streamflow that
it shifts the creek's conservative-tracer chemistry (chloride)
measurably while barely shifting its bulk isotopic signature, which
stays dominated by meteoric water.

```{r fig-evolution}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/fluid_evolution_flowpath.png",
  "Real chemistry, PHREEQC saturation indices, geothermometer estimates, and stable isotopes across the sampled Lower Sinter Terrace flowpath, from the two reconstructed parent fluids through measured discharge, a nearby well, and the two Steamboat Creek chloride-mass-balance stations.",
  alt = "Twelve-panel scatter plot showing chloride, sodium, sulfate, silica, boron, pH, calcite and quartz saturation indices, two geothermometer estimates, and two stable isotopes across seven real or reconstructed flowpath nodes.",
  id = "fig-evolution"
)
```

The three real, independently sampled thermal points (fissure, resort
tank, nearby well) give sodium/potassium reservoir-temperature
estimates of 173.4, 179.2, and 180.2 degrees Celsius -- a 6.8-degree
range and a 2.1 percent coefficient of variation. Three points is too
few for a formally powered statistical test, stated plainly rather than
dressed up with an inappropriate p-value, but a spread this tight
relative to the 50-100 degree Celsius divergence this project's own
geothermometer-vs-measured-temperature comparison already documents
across its full real sample set is a real, specific piece of evidence
consistent with these three points sharing one deep source, not three
independent ones.

**What the geothermometers say about hot and dissolving zones in the
shallow subsurface.** Reading the Na/K estimate, the quartz-
equilibration estimate, and the measured discharge temperature
together for all six real thermal features (not just the three used
for the agreement test above) turns the geothermometer divergence
already documented in Chapter 2 into a real diagnostic. At every
single feature, quartz equilibration (99-127 degrees Celsius) sits
above the measured discharge temperature, and Na/K (173-190 degrees
Celsius) sits higher still -- a real, three-stage cooling signature:
a shared deep reservoir around 175-190 degrees Celsius (Na/K, slow to
re-equilibrate), transit through a shallower zone still hot enough to
leave a quartz signature well above final discharge temperature, then
a last, near-surface step down to whatever temperature is actually
measured at the tap or pool. The SIZE of that last step is not uniform
across feature types, and it lines up with the gain/loss pattern
below: the two coolest real springs (SBS_0001, 47.8 degrees Celsius;
SBS_0003, 39.6 degrees Celsius) show the largest gap between their
quartz estimate and their measured temperature (79 and 63 degrees
Celsius respectively), while the wells (SBW_0001, SBF_0001) show a
smaller gap (28-51 degrees Celsius) despite starting from a similar
quartz-equilibration temperature. Read together with the sulfate-gain/
alkalinity-loss pattern below, this is consistent with the springs
undergoing more near-surface processing -- more cooling, more
atmosphere-driven chemical change -- on the way to discharge than the
wells do, even though all of these features' deeper temperatures agree
closely. This does not identify a specific hot zone or dissolving zone
with a depth or a coordinate -- that would need real well-log or
geophysical data this project does not yet have (Chapter 3) -- but it
does say, with real numbers, that the shallow subsurface is not
thermally or chemically uniform between discharge points, and that
springs and wells experience that non-uniformity differently.

**A conceptual figure, informed by visual inspection of the thermal-infrared
surveys already shared for this project.** @fig-conceptual lays out the
full flowpath as a schematic: deep parent fluid, degassing, the three
real measured discharge points, shallow meteoric mixing, Steamboat
Creek at SBRR, White's [-@white1968c] own documented approximately
100 gallon-per-minute "unseen" Lower Sinter Terrace thermal inflow
between SBRR and SBBV (notebook section 4.7), Steamboat Creek at SBBV,
and the downstream conductivity logger/United States Geological Survey
gauge. The calibrated thermal-infrared imagery already shared for this
project (a July-versus-October 2025 comparison, and a separate
calibrated orthophoto) shows two visually distinct kinds of warm
signature: discrete, persistent point sources along the terrace's
western margin (plausible active degassing/boiling vents, stable
between the two survey dates) and a broader, more diffuse warm
signature tracking the creek channel itself (more consistent with
shallow seepage and mixing than point-source degassing). This is
stated as a qualitative, visual read of imagery already in hand, not a
digitized layer -- the underlying raster files are not yet on disk
(see `docs/action_items_for_user.md`, item 12) -- and is offered here
as a real, if provisional, answer to what can be said before that
digitization work happens: the system appears to have at least two
physically distinct discharge styles operating side by side on the
same terrace, which is itself a testable prediction for the planned
spring/seep remapping fieldwork.

```{r fig-conceptual}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/lst_conceptual_flowpath.png",
  "Conceptual flowpath from the reconstructed deep parent fluid through degassing, the three real measured discharge points, shallow meteoric mixing, Steamboat Creek, and the downstream conductivity logger, with real chloride values annotated at each node.",
  alt = "Schematic box-and-arrow diagram showing the conceptual flowpath from a deep parent fluid through degassing and discharge points to Steamboat Creek and a downstream conductivity logger.",
  id = "fig-conceptual"
)
```

NV26-2's flagged contamination is a concrete, low-cost lesson for the
sampling plan above, not just a data-quality footnote: future
Giggenbach-bottle gas sampling at this terrace should avoid breaking
through fresh pavement and should re-check bottle seals in the field
before leaving the site.

## A baseline chemical-evolution characterization of the flowpath

Everything in this subsection is read from the mixing, reaction-path,
and geothermometer runs already reported above -- no new PHREEQC
execution was needed. The real samples feeding every result here were
all collected within the same field season, so this is explicitly a
**one-time, same-era baseline characterization**: a demonstration that
this modeling approach can reconstruct mixing, chemical evolution, and
feature-type connectivity along a real flowpath from a single snapshot
of real data, not an iterative refinement project. Further precision --
tighter end-members, a real paired uncertainty estimate for inverse
modeling, resolving SBS_0001's own unresolved tension -- is explicitly
deferred to the same-day synoptic sampling round proposed in Chapter 5,
not pursued further here. What follows connects this fissure-specific
work directly to the broader chloride-conductivity proxy work: both
are, at bottom, asking how far, and in what chemical form, the same
thermal signal travels from its source.

**How much of each discharge point is fissure-strength fluid, and how
does that connect to the downstream proxy record?** Using the real,
already-computed Cl-based mixing fraction against the fissure and SBRR
end-members, shown in @fig-mixingfraction, the three real Low Sinter
Terrace springs and seep sit at 0.77-0.89 (mostly fissure-strength
fluid, diluted only modestly), the nearby well (SBW_0001) sits lower
at 0.57, and the resort tank exceeds the fissure reference itself
(1.04, already documented as a real finding, not an error). SBRR
itself anchors the dilute end by definition; its downstream partner
SBBV, several kilometers further down Steamboat Creek, still implies
about 14 percent fissure-strength fluid by chloride alone -- the same
real signal, at a much smaller concentration, that
`chloride_mass_balance.R`'s own 58.7 liter-per-second thermal-discharge
estimate is built on. This is the direct link between the fissure-
specific chemistry above and the creek-scale conductivity-as-proxy
work: the same conservative mixing framework explains both.

```{r fig-mixingfraction}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/mixing_fraction_by_target.png",
  "Real Cl-based mixing fraction (fraction fissure end-member) for every real downgradient target, colored by feature type.",
  alt = "Horizontal bar chart of mixing fraction for six real targets, sorted from SBBV (lowest) to the resort tank (highest, exceeding 1).",
  id = "fig-mixingfraction"
)
```

**What is gained or lost, species by species, and does it distinguish
feature types?** Comparing each real target's measured chemistry
against what the same Cl-based mixing fraction would predict if every
species traveled conservatively, shown in @fig-gainloss, sodium comes
back essentially conservative everywhere (within 6 percent), the
direct justification for treating chloride and sodium as reliable
tracers in this system. Potassium is modestly gained everywhere (13-31
percent), a real, open signal plausibly reflecting mild clay or
feldspar exchange, not chased further here. Sulfate and alkalinity are
where the real feature-type distinction shows up, sharpened in
@fig-springswells: **every spring and the seep gain far more sulfate
relative to conservative mixing than either well** (44-62 percent
versus -3 to 20 percent), and alkalinity is **gained at both wells but
lost at two of the three springs** -- opposite signs for the same
species, split cleanly along feature type. Plausible mechanisms for
both: open spring and seep discharge points are exposed to the
atmosphere in a way a cased well is not, so near-surface oxidation of
residual hydrogen sulfide to sulfate, and carbon dioxide degassing
that would otherwise support alkalinity, both have more opportunity to
happen before a sample is ever collected.

```{r fig-gainloss}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/species_gainloss_heatmap.png",
  "Real measured concentration versus the conservative-mixing prediction for six species, for every real downgradient target, expressed as percent gained or lost.",
  alt = "Tile plot with targets on rows and species on columns, colored and labeled by percent deviation from conservative mixing.",
  id = "fig-gainloss"
)
```

```{r fig-springswells}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/springs_vs_wells_residuals.png",
  "Sulfate and alkalinity gain/loss relative to conservative mixing, grouped by feature type, isolating the clearest feature-type pattern from the full heatmap above.",
  alt = "Two-panel bar chart, one panel for alkalinity and one for sulfate, bars colored by feature type (well, well resort, spring, seep).",
  id = "fig-springswells"
)
```

**How does the real temperature record fit into this, and is this a
chemically feasible connection for every feature type, or not?** The
three-stage cooling picture in @fig-tempprofile (Na/K reservoir
estimate, quartz-equilibration estimate, measured discharge
temperature) and the Steamboat Creek re-warming between SBRR and SBBV
are both drawn directly from values already reported above, placed
side by side here as the clearest single summary figure for this
subsection. Put all of this together and the honest answer is neither
a clean "yes, connected" nor a clean "no, not connected": the real
Na/K reservoir-temperature agreement (173-190 degrees Celsius across
every real thermal feature, not just the three used for the formal
agreement test above) is consistent with one shared deep source
feeding wells, springs, and the seep alike. But the sulfate, alkalinity,
and quartz-versus-measured-temperature patterns above show that
**springs and wells diverge systematically in near-surface process**,
not randomly -- springs and the seep show more cooling below their own
quartz-equilibration temperature and a consistent sulfate-gain/
alkalinity-loss signature that the wells do not share. The more precise
and more defensible statement, given this real baseline snapshot, is
that these features are chemically consistent with a shared deep
source but **not** chemically consistent with identical near-surface
pathways -- a real, specific, testable distinction between spring-type
and well-type connectivity that a simple proximity map alone (SBS_0001
and SBW_0001 sit only 109 meters apart yet show two of the most
different fit behaviors on this flowpath, already noted above) cannot
provide on its own.

```{r fig-tempprofile}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/temperature_flowpath_profile.png",
  "A. Three-stage cooling (Na/K reservoir estimate, quartz-equilibration estimate, measured discharge) for all six real thermal features, colored by feature type. B. Steamboat Creek's real measured temperature rise from SBRR to SBBV.",
  alt = "Two-panel figure: a line plot of temperature across three cooling stages for six features colored by type, and a two-point line plot showing creek temperature rising downstream.",
  id = "fig-tempprofile"
)
```


## Further cross-checks: water/gas geothermometers, facies, and discharge

**Water and gas geothermometers side by side.** Putting the gas
geothermometer estimates next to this project's existing water
geothermometers (Na/K-Giggenbach, Na/K-Fournier, quartz, chalcedony;
132 real method/sample estimates across 63 thermal samples with complete
chemistry) against measured temperature, shown in @fig-geothermwatergas,
makes the pattern explicit rather than described only in prose: every
method except quartz and chalcedony over-predicts measured
temperature, and the one real co-located point (NV26-1 gas / SBF_0001
water) sits consistently with that pattern rather than as an outlier --
the gas estimate (228 degrees Celsius) lands closest to the Na/K
estimates (153-173 degrees Celsius) among the water methods, not the
quartz/chalcedony pair (92-118 degrees Celsius), suggesting both the
gas and the Na/K-based water signatures are responding to a similar,
deeper and hotter part of the system than the silica-based estimates.

```{r fig-geothermwatergas}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/gas_analysis/geothermometer_water_gas_comparison.png",
  "Water and gas geothermometer estimates vs. measured temperature, all real thermal samples. Already produced.",
  alt = "Scatter plot of geothermometer-estimated temperature versus measured temperature, colored by method, with the one real co-located gas/water point labeled.",
  id = "fig-geothermwatergas"
)
```

**A first real PHREEQC test using the gas data.** The gas isotope and
conservative-ratio data collected here are also a natural input to the
PHREEQC gas-phase modeling already described in the Background
section -- and, for the first time, a real test was possible rather
than only a synthetic self-test: SBF_0001's real water chemistry was
re-equilibrated against a `GAS_PHASE` seeded with NV26-1's real,
air-corrected CO2-to-H2S proportions (96.5 to 3.5 percent) at 1
atmosphere, modeled as an open system continuously resupplied by the
fissure. Shown in @fig-gasphase, the result is a real, substantive
shift: pH drops from the water's measured 8.3 to a modeled 5.7, and
calcite, aragonite, and dolomite all move from supersaturated (as this
project's PHREEQC pipeline already finds for the water alone) to
undersaturated. Read plainly, this says the water as sampled is not
simply sitting in equilibrium with the vent gas as sampled -- either
the two were not collected from truly the same fluid parcel, gas and
liquid separate before either is caught at the surface, or the real
reservoir pressure (not the 1 atmosphere used here as a simplification)
changes the picture. Any of those is a real, useful constraint on how
this system's gas and water should eventually be modeled together, not
a result to over-interpret from one sample pair.

```{r fig-gasphase}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/gas_analysis/gas_phase_fischer_pairing_before_after.png",
  "SBF_0001 water chemistry before and after PHREEQC equilibration with a real GAS_PHASE seeded from NV26-1's measured composition. Already produced.",
  alt = "Bar chart comparing pH and three carbonate mineral saturation indices before and after equilibrating a real water sample with a real measured gas composition.",
  id = "fig-gasphase"
)
```

**Hydrochemical facies recover known geochemistry.** Clustering every
real sample with complete major-ion chemistry, independently
cross-checked by principal component analysis and a classification
method, recovers a pure sodium-chloride thermal cluster, a dilute
background-water cluster, and an intermediate mixed cluster, without
being told each sample's site type in advance -- three independent
statistical approaches converging on the same chemical structure, as
shown in @fig-facies.

```{r fig-facies}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/facies/facies_pca_biplot.png",
  "Principal-component biplot of major-ion chemistry, colored by persisted hydrochemical-facies cluster assignment. Already produced.",
  alt = "Principal component biplot of major-ion chemistry, points colored by hydrochemical facies cluster, showing thermal, mixed, and background groups.",
  id = "fig-facies"
)
```

**A real, database-grounded discharge estimate.** Applying the
chloride mass-balance method to the one real date with paired
chloride and discharge measurements at both gauging stations gives
58.7 liters per second, a single-day value that sits within, not
clearly above or below, the broader 1955-2026 record (roughly
30-90 L/s depending on year and method) once Sorey and Spielman's own
documented seasonal variability is taken into account, shown in
@fig-discharge.

```{r fig-discharge}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/discharge_through_time.png",
  "Thermal-water discharge to Steamboat Creek, 1955-2026. Already produced.",
  alt = "Line and point plot of estimated thermal-water discharge to Steamboat Creek from 1955 to 2026.",
  id = "fig-discharge"
)
```

## Sampling-frequency feasibility and recent monitoring time series

**Sampling-frequency feasibility.** The Monte Carlo result described
in the Methods section above and shown in @fig-mc is itself a
completed preliminary analysis, not a planned one.

```{r fig-mc}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/sampling_frequency_error_curve.png",
  "Monte Carlo reconstruction-error curve for candidate chemistry-sampling intervals. Already produced.",
  alt = "Line plot of Monte Carlo reconstruction error versus chemistry-sampling interval, from daily to biweekly sampling.",
  id = "fig-mc"
)
```

**A real three-month field-parameter time series.** A roughly monthly
record of pH, temperature, and specific conductance across fourteen
sites -- six injection-side ports and eight shallow monitoring and
domestic wells -- spanning late September through December 2025 shows
a stable, consistent gap between the injection-side ports (pH 5.8-6.3)
and the shallow well network (pH 7.0-8.1), present in every round
rather than as a single-date artifact. Two individual wells also show
real, opposite-direction multi-month trends not explained by any
change in the other monitored parameter at the same well, a pattern
that cautions against treating any single field parameter as a
universal proxy for thermal fraction across the whole system.

**An extended conductivity record, and a recurring instrument-handling
artifact now caught automatically.** Both stream conductivity loggers
(SBRR and SBGG) were re-downloaded October 12, 2026, extending the
continuous record from 2026-08-22 through 2026-10-10 and nearly
doubling the total logger-observation count on file. The new data show
the same recurring pattern already documented at the prior
2026-08-22 download: when a logger is physically removed from the
stream to connect a shuttle and then relaunched, it briefly reads
ambient air instead of stream water, producing a sharp, implausible
drop in specific conductance immediately before and after the
retrieval/relaunch event (@fig-conductivity-timeseries). Rather than
re-flag this by hand a second time, a general detector was added to
this project's conductivity QC script that scans for exactly this
signature -- a reading that falls below a fraction of the local stable
baseline immediately adjacent to a deployment-start marker or a large
time gap -- and flags it automatically (`qc_flag =
'field_visit_disturbance'`). Applied retroactively, the new detector
reproduces every previously hand-flagged row exactly and additionally
catches a short relaunch-related dip on 2026-08-22 and the full width
of the 2026-10-10 retrieval excursion that a simple point-outlier
check alone would have missed. This means every future logger download
will be checked for the same artifact automatically, rather than
requiring a manual review each time.

```{r fig-conductivity-timeseries}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/conductivity_timeseries.png",
  "Full SBRR/SBGG conductivity record, 2026-07-15 to 2026-10-10, with the automatically detected ambient-air-exposure artifact highlighted in orange at both the 2026-08-22 and 2026-10-10 retrieval/relaunch events.",
  alt = "Two-panel time series of raw specific conductance at SBGG and SBRR, with orange points marking flagged retrieval-artifact readings near two dates.",
  id = "fig-conductivity-timeseries"
)
```

**A still-changing system: September 2026 field observations.** Field
photographs taken September 27, 2026 (GPS- and time-stamped by camera
EXIF data, all within about 150 meters of each other at the terrace)
document that the system has continued to change since the 2026
poster was presented. First, a new seep-fed hot spring, shown in
@fig-hotspring, is now discharging among bedrock boulders at a
location that was not an active feature previously; a nearby resident
independently confirmed that this is a new development, consistent
with the thesis's own field observation rather than resting on a
single observer's judgment. Second, a native-sulfur deposit at the
terrace, shown in @fig-sulfur, has visibly grown in size and remains
texturally fresh, again by both the resident's account and direct
observation -- a real, physical sign of continuing near-surface
fumarolic input, not a static relic of the 2025 event. Third, a
separate point at the terrace, shown in @fig-seep, shows a seep
discharging from the alluvial cover directly onto the underlying hard
sinter bedrock outcrop, a concrete example of the alluvium-to-bedrock
contact this thesis's own spring and well remapping is designed to
document systematically rather than opportunistically. Together,
these three observations are read as further, independent support for
the poster's own conclusion -- fluids continuing to redistribute
within an existing shallow conduit system, rather than the system
having settled into a new, static state since the 2025 eruption -- and
they are a direct, concrete motivation for why the remapping and
monitoring work proposed below needs to happen now rather than later.

```{r fig-hotspring}

  alt = "Photograph of a new seep discharging warm water among bedrock boulders toward Steamboat Creek.",
  id = "fig-hotspring"
)
```

```{r fig-sulfur}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/field_photo_sulfur_deposit_20260927.jpg",
  "A fresh, visibly growing native-sulfur deposit (yellow) along the Steamboat Creek bank, photographed September 27, 2026 (39.3805, -119.7396).",
  alt = "Photograph of a bright yellow native-sulfur deposit along a creek bank, with white sinter crust surrounding it.",
  id = "fig-sulfur"
)
```

## Planned figures, not yet produced

Three figures central to the finished thesis cannot be produced yet,
and are described here rather than filled with a placeholder or an
unrepresentative result.

**A real chloride-conductivity calibration plot** (chloride
concentration versus specific conductance, with a fitted regression
line and confidence band, by site type) will be the thesis's central
figure. It requires the paired chloride-and-conductance samples the
sampling plan above is designed to collect, and cannot be produced from
the current, unpaired records.

**A monitoring-network map** showing production, injection, and
monitoring wells together with mapped structure and lithology will
provide the geologic context described above. It awaits the
digitized fault geometry discussed in the geologic-context section.

**A final conceptual model** of the Lower Sinter Terrace system,
synthesizing the chemical, discharge, and geologic evidence into a
single interpretive diagram, will be developed once the calibration,
tracer-ratio, and geologic-context results above are complete -- it
is deliberately not sketched in advance of that evidence.

**A thermal-infrared/mapped-feature overlay map.** NBMG's own
calibrated nighttime thermal-infrared drone surveys of the Lower
Sinter Terrace (flown 2025-07-07/08 and 2025-10-01, per Lindsey and
others 2026) would, overlaid against three other real, already-
database-resident point layers, directly test whether this project's
mapped surface thermal anomalies line up with (a) the 32 historically
mapped wells, springs, and fissures newly ingested from the White/
Geyser Society GIS sheet in this chapter's Methods, (b) the 51 real,
GPS-tagged `SBO_*` Lower Sinter Terrace survey points from this
project's own 2026 field remapping (28 seeps, 13 steaming-ground
observations, 7 springs, 3 creek points), and (c) any other dated
field observation with a real coordinate in the `Locations` table.
The question this map answers is whether the current surface thermal
signature is concentrated at historically documented features (support
for conduit reactivation along known pathways) or has migrated to new
ground not previously mapped as thermal (which would argue for a less
constrained, more diffuse redistribution). This map is not yet built:
the thermal-infrared raster files themselves are not on disk in this
project (confirmed directly -- no `.tif`/`.tiff` file exists anywhere
under `data/raw/`, and no public repository hosting them was found);
they exist today only as images shared informally and still need to be
requested directly from NBMG. The three point layers it would overlay
against are themselves already real and mappable today.

**The three September 27, 2026 field photographs** above (@fig-hotspring,
@fig-sulfur, @fig-seep) carry real GPS coordinates and timestamps in
their own camera EXIF data, confirmed directly rather than assumed,
but have not yet been run through this project's formal photo-location
ingestion pipeline to become real, dated `Locations` entries in the
underlying database -- that promotion step, not the figures
themselves, is the remaining task. The earlier-visit photo of this
same seep used in @fig-seep-compare and the SBGG installation photo in
@fig-sbgg-install are real field images from this project's own work
but, unlike the three September 27 photos, their EXIF metadata no
longer carries a capture date or GPS fix (confirmed directly via
exiftool, not assumed) -- both await the same ingestion-pipeline
promotion once a real coordinate and date are recovered or
re-recorded.

# Preliminary schedule

The schedule below moves the intensive calibration window up to this
fall/winter (rather than a conventional spring field-season start) and
stretches monthly chloride sampling across a full annual cycle, so the
calibration can be tested against all four seasons before it is
treated as final, consistent with the sampling-design reasoning above.
Target dates are a planning structure, not fixed commitments, and will
be adjusted against the real academic calendar and committee
availability as the work proceeds. The most direct risk to this
schedule is weather- or access-limited fieldwork during the
fall/winter calibration window; the contingency is the same full-year
monthly cadence shifted later into spring/summer 2027, at the cost of
testing fewer distinct seasons before the calibration is finalized.
A second risk is that the real chloride-conductance relationship
turns out to be too noisy or site-specific to support a single
practical calibration; the contingency there is reported directly in
RQ1's own deliverable above (site-specific equations with stated
uncertainty, not a forced single model) rather than treated as a
schedule failure.

| Target date | Milestone |
|---|---|
| Oct-Nov 2026 | Submit this proposal and program of study; begin the intensive daily-to-sub-daily Cl-conductance calibration window at SBRR/SBGG (moved up from a spring 2027 start, since the conductivity loggers are already running); continue spring and well remapping at the Lower Sinter Terrace. |
| Dec 2026 | First monthly chloride sample of the full-year cadence (early winter baseflow conditions). |
| Jan 2027 | Monthly chloride sample; winter-season logger maintenance and remapping. |
| Feb 2027 | Monthly chloride sample. |
| Mar 2027 | Monthly chloride sample; watch for early spring runoff onset. |
| Apr 2027 | Monthly chloride sample, with additional unscheduled samples around spring snowmelt/runoff, when the Cl-conductance relationship is most likely to shift. |
| May 2027 | Monthly chloride sample; isotope sampling on the prioritized subset. |
| Jun 2027 | Monthly chloride sample; roughly one full year of continuous conductance logging completed; mid-candidacy committee check-in and preliminary-results presentation. |
| Jul 2027 | Monthly chloride sample; begin fitting a preliminary seasonal calibration now that a full annual cycle of paired samples exists. |
| Aug 2027 | Monthly chloride sample; evaluate calibration residuals by season (winter vs. runoff vs. summer vs. fall). |
| Sep 2027 | Final monthly chloride sample of the full-year campaign (the twelfth month); finalize the chloride-conductance calibration, both site-specific and global models. |
| Oct 2027 | Complete the PHREEQC conservativeness and endmember-stability analyses; apply the post-eruption discharge and tracer-ratio interpretation. |
| Nov 2027 | Finalize the geologic-context framework; begin the full thesis-writing push. |
| Dec 2027 | Complete thesis writing, defend, and submit. |

# Expected products

- A real chloride-to-specific-conductance calibration equation, or set
  of site-specific equations, with stated uncertainty.
- A quantitative minimum-sampling-frequency recommendation for
  ongoing chloride monitoring at Steamboat.
- A PHREEQC-based physical justification -- or documented limitation
  -- for using specific conductance as a chloride proxy at this site.
- An updated interpretation of thermal-water discharge and conservative-
  tracer behavior before and after the 2025 eruption.
- Two candidate manuscripts: *Conductivity-Based Monitoring of
  Chloride Discharge at Steamboat Hills* (targeting *Geothermics* or
  *Geothermal Energy*), and *Hydrochemical Evolution of the Lower
  Sinter Terrace System Following the 2025 Eruption* (drawing on the
  PHREEQC, tracer-ratio, and historical-comparison results above).
- A three-dimensional conceptual geologic framework for the monitored
  wells and springs, explicitly scoped as context rather than a flow
  model.

# Conclusion

This proposal answers a question Sorey originally posed and this
project's own 2026 poster [@irvinlindsey2026] re-asked after the 2025
eruption: is Steamboat's renewed activity a new thermal source, or an
old one finding a new way out? The poster's own evidence -- matching
chemistry, a strong inverse relationship between paired temperature
loggers, and continuing physical change at the terrace through at
least September 2026 -- points toward the latter, but that evidence
was gathered at poster speed, not thesis speed: a handful of samples,
one representative mixing pair, and no real chloride-conductance
calibration yet. What changes once this work is done is that the
same question gets a real, stated-uncertainty answer instead of a
preliminary one. A working chloride-to-conductance calibration turns
a labor-intensive, infrequent sampling program into a continuous,
field-deployable monitoring tool -- not just for this thesis, but for
whoever manages this system's monitoring network after it. A
PHREEQC-based accounting of why conductance should or should not track
chloride turns that tool from a correlation into something with a
stated physical basis and known limits. And a real, if still partial,
three-dimensional geologic framework starts to connect the chemistry
to the structure it is moving through, rather than leaving the two
literatures to talk past each other. None of this closes the book on
Steamboat -- the system is still visibly changing, as the September
2026 field observations above show -- but it leaves whoever studies it
next with a real, working method for tracking that change, rather
than another one-time estimate.
